n: Two years after the vision of the four beasts, Daniel receives another. From this chapter to the end, the book returns to Hebrew. This vision zooms in on the second and third kingdoms of chapter 7.

f.w: the third year of the reign of king Belshazzar
f.g: About 551 BC. Daniel 8–12 is written in Hebrew.

f.w: that which appeared unto me at the first

n: In vision Daniel finds himself at Shushan (Susa), a royal city in Elam that would become a Persian capital, beside the Ulai canal.

f.g: Susa, later a capital of the Persian Empire.
A region east of Babylon, in modern southwestern Iran.

n: A ram with two horns, one taller than the other, which grew up last—Media and Persia, with Persia becoming dominant later.

f.w: a ram which had two horns

n: The ram charges west, north, and south, and no one can stop it. The Persian Empire expanded in all these directions.
A male goat from the west races across the earth so fast its feet don’t touch the ground. It has one prominent horn between its eyes—Alexander the Great.

f.g: A male goat.
A conspicuous, prominent horn.

n: The goat charges the ram in furious power.
It strikes the ram, shatters both horns, and tramples it. Alexander defeated the Persian Empire in a series of battles from 334 to 331 BC.

f.g: Rage, fury.

n: At the height of its power, the great horn breaks, and four horns grow in its place. Alexander died suddenly in 323 BC, and his empire was split among four of his generals.

f.g: Grew.

n: From one of these comes a “little horn” that grows toward the south, east, and “the pleasant land”—Israel. Most scholars identify this ruler with Antiochus IV Epiphanes of the Seleucid kingdom (175–164 BC).

f.g: The beautiful land—the land of Israel.

n: It grows so arrogant that it attacks the host of heaven, throwing some stars down and trampling them—probably God’s faithful people, pictured as stars.
It even challenges the Prince of the host—God Himself—stopping the daily sacrifice and defiling the sanctuary. Antiochus did ban temple sacrifices in Jerusalem in 167 BC.

f.g: The continual morning and evening offerings.
Exalted himself, acted with arrogance.

n: Because of transgression, the horn is allowed to overpower the sacrifice and throw truth to the ground. For a time, evil seems to prosper.

f.g: Did as it pleased and succeeded.

n: Daniel hears two holy ones asking, “How long will this desecration last?” It is the cry of the suffering faithful in every age.

f.g: Holy one—an angel.
The sin that causes horror and ruin.

n: The answer: 2,300 “evenings and mornings,” then the sanctuary will be restored. This may mean 1,150 days (counting evening and morning sacrifices) or 2,300 days. The Maccabees rededicated the temple in 164 BC—the origin of Hanukkah.

f.w: two thousand and three hundred days
f.g: Literally “evening-morning” 2,300—possibly 1,150 days of missed sacrifices.

f.w: then shall the sanctuary be cleansed
f.g: Restored to its right condition.

n: As Daniel seeks understanding, someone who looks like a man appears before him.
A voice calls from the Ulai: “Gabriel, explain the vision to this man.” This is the first time an angel is named in the Bible. Latter-day Saints understand Gabriel to be Noah.

f.g: Hebrew “God is my strength” (or “man of God”).

n: Daniel falls on his face in fear. Gabriel calls him “son of man” (mortal) and says the vision concerns “the time of the end.”
Daniel collapses into a deep stupor, but the angel touches him and raises him to his feet.

f.w: he touched me, and set me upright

n: Gabriel will explain what happens at the end of the period of wrath—at the time God has appointed.

f.g: The period of God’s wrath or of persecution.

n: The two-horned ram is the kings of Media and Persia.
The goat is the king of Greece; the great horn is its first king—Alexander.

f.g: Greece (Hebrew Yavan).

n: The four horns are four kingdoms that arise from his empire, but none as powerful as he was.
Late in their rule, when wickedness reaches its full measure, a fierce king skilled in intrigue will arise.

f.g: Skilled in riddles, intrigue, or deceit.

f.w: when the transgressors are come to the full

n: His power will be great, but not his own—permitted by God. He will cause astonishing destruction and persecute God’s holy people.
Through cunning he will make deceit prosper, exalt himself, and destroy many who feel safe. He will even oppose the Prince of princes—but he will be broken “without hand,” by God, not by human power.

f.g: God; Christians see Christ as Prince of princes.

f.w: he shall be broken without hand

f.g: Cunning, shrewdness.

n: The vision of the evenings and mornings is true. Daniel must “shut up” (seal and preserve) it, because it concerns the distant future.
Daniel is exhausted and ill for days. Then he gets up and returns to the king’s business—faithful in daily duties even while bewildered by what he saw.

f.w: I Daniel fainted, and was sick certain days
